issues.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to the victim does not, by itself, make the witness an interested witness.
material_facts: The witness was the deceased’s wife and was present with him when the attack occurred.
She was the only eyewitness and a natural witness in the circumstances.
A land dispute existed between the deceased’s family and the accused, but the court found no interest on the witness’s part in protecting the real culprit or falsely implicating the accused.
issues.conclusion: The witness could not be treated as interested merely because she was related to the deceased.
issues.legal_principle: A witness is not interested simply because the witness is related to a party or victim. A witness is interested when the witness derives some benefit from the outcome, such as a civil decree or seeing an accused punished. A natural witness who is the only possible eyewitness is not, for that reason, interested. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and witness_is_related_to_victim and witness_is_natural_sole_eyewitness and not witness_derives_benefit_from_conviction

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which witness evidence is assessed.
predicates.witness_is_related_to_victim: The witness is related to the person who was harmed or killed.
predicates.witness_is_natural_sole_eyewitness: The witness was naturally present in the circumstances and was the only eyewitness.
predicates.witness_derives_benefit_from_conviction: The witness would derive a benefit from the outcome, such as a civil decree or the punishment of the accused.

issues.definition: When a related witness is the natural sole eyewitness in a criminal prosecution and derives no benefit from conviction, the relationship alone does not make the witness interested.

issues.legal_issue: Minor, normal, or explainable discrepancies in testimony are not material discrepancies warranting rejection of the testimony.
material_facts: The witness’s evidence differed on details including who pressed the deceased to the ground, where the deceased was pressed, whether the fatal blow was delivered while he was standing or lying down, and the direction from which the blow was given.
The court regarded these differences as minor and natural, consistent with ordinary errors of observation or memory and the effects of shock and horror.
The medical evidence supported the witness’s account of an axe blow to the neck.
issues.conclusion: The discrepancies were not material and did not justify rejecting the witness’s evidence in its entirety.
issues.legal_principle: Witnesses may have normal discrepancies arising from errors of observation, memory, lapse of time, or mental disposition such as shock and horror. Material discrepancies are those that are not normal or expected of a normal person. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.criminal_evidence_assessment: The court is assessing testimony in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.testimony_contains_discrepancies: The witness’s account differs on some details of the occurrence.
predicates.discrepancies_are_minor_normal_or_explai: The differences concern details and are ordinary or explainable by observation, memory, lapse of time, or the witness’s mental state.

issues.definition: When discrepancies in testimony in a criminal proceeding are minor, normal, or explainable, the testimony is not rejected as materially discrepant.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under its special-leave jurisdiction with factual findings that border on perversity and result in a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The matter was a special-leave appeal against an acquittal.
The High Court rejected the eyewitness’s evidence on grounds the Supreme Court found invalid, treating relationship as proof of interest and minor discrepancies as material.
The Supreme Court found that the acquittal resulted in a grave miscarriage of justice.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court interfered with the factual findings, set aside the acquittal, and restored criminal liability.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court normally does not interfere with findings of fact made by the High Court. It may do so when those findings border on perversity and result in a miscarriage of justice. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_against_acquittal and high_court_made_factual_findings and findings_border_on_perversity and findings_result_in_miscarriage_of_justice

predicates.special_leave_appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is a special-leave appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.high_court_made_factual_findings: The High Court made findings of fact in deciding the case.
predicates.findings_border_on_perversity: The factual findings are so unreasonable that they border on perversity.
predicates.findings_result_in_miscarriage_of_justic: The factual findings produce a miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal against an acquittal challenges High Court findings that border on perversity and cause a miscarriage of justice, the Supreme Court may interfere with those findings.

issues.legal_issue: Eyewitness evidence supported by medical evidence and other evidence of the accused’s conduct can establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt for the fatal attack and participation in it.
material_facts: The deceased’s homicidal death was undisputed.
The sole eyewitness testified that one accused delivered the fatal axe blow to the deceased’s neck.
The medical officer found an incised wound on the neck consistent with that account.
Another witness saw the accused leaving the scene with weapons.
The evidence showed that the other accused came armed, called the deceased out, and helped bring him down so that the fatal attack could be carried out.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution proved the guilt of both accused beyond reasonable doubt; one was convicted for the killing and the other for participation with common intention.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the requirements for murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and for liability with common intention under Section 302 read with Section 34, finding the prosecution evidence sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_acquittal and eyewitness_identifies_fatal_attacker and medical_evidence_supports_account and other_evidence_corrobates_attack_and_participation

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.eyewitness_identifies_fatal_attacker: An eyewitness identifies an accused as delivering the fatal blow.
predicates.medical_evidence_supports_account: Medical findings are consistent with the eyewitness’s account of the fatal injury.
predicates.other_evidence_corrobates_attack_and_par: Other evidence supports the account of the attack and the accused’s participation in it.

issues.definition: When an eyewitness identifies the fatal attacker, medical evidence supports that account, and other evidence corroborates the attack and participation in a criminal appeal against acquittal, guilt is established beyond reasonable doubt.
